subject: Chemistry
title: LEDs: Light From Semiconductors
description: A micro-lesson that makes LEDs: Light From Semiconductors usable.

hook.text: LEDs produce light when electrons drop across a semiconductor bandgap. Different gaps give different colors.

buildup.text: In an LED, electrons cross from a high-energy layer to a low-energy layer. The energy difference is emitted as a photon.

discovery.text: Red LEDs came in 1962. Green followed. But blue was the problem—no one could make a wide-bandgap semiconductor work.

twist.text: Shuji Nakamura cracked blue LEDs in 1994 using gallium nitride. He won the Nobel Prize in 2014 for enabling white LEDs.

climax.text: White LEDs combine blue LED light with a yellow phosphor coating. They use 85% less energy than incandescent bulbs.

punchline.text: Electrons fall across a gap, photons fly out. Semiconductor physics makes light.

quiz.question: Why was the blue LED so important?
options: It enabled white LEDs by combining blue light with yellow phosphor
Blue light carries more energy than other colors
It was the first LED that could be seen in daylight

details.summary: Light-emitting diodes produce color when electrons cross a semiconductor junction and recombine with holes, releasing energy as photons. The photon wavelength, and therefore the LED color, is determined by the semiconductor's band gap, with different materials producing different colors.
details.whyItMatters: LEDs have transformed global energy consumption by replacing incandescent bulbs with devices that are up to ninety percent more efficient. Blue LED development earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
takeaways: Electron-hole recombination across a band gap produces colored photons
Different semiconductor materials produce different LED colors
Blue LEDs completed the RGB set needed for white LED lighting

faq.question: Why was the blue LED so much harder to develop than red and green?
faq.answer: Red and green LEDs used well-understood gallium arsenide and gallium phosphide semiconductors. Blue LEDs required gallium nitride, which was extremely difficult to grow as high-quality crystals. It took decades of research to solve the crystal growth and doping challenges.

faq.question: How do white LEDs actually produce white light from a single color?
faq.answer: Most white LEDs use a blue LED chip coated with yellow phosphor. The blue light excites the phosphor, which emits broad-spectrum yellow light. The combination of blue and yellow light appears white to the human eye. Higher quality LEDs use multiple phosphors for better color rendering.
